title: Zeno's lost books
hook: Zeno wrote many books, almost all lost; we know him through others (Diogenes Laërtius 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: know again, twelve books read straight through. Your line was read it again. Which passage did you choose for your mornings? Day six hundred forty-one.

An ancient biographer copied out a long list of one man's book titles. Not one of those books can be found today. All anyone knows of their author comes from what others said about him, centuries later, some of them people who never met him, some of them rivals. That's the situation of the man who started it all. For months we've read Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus, the Roman Stoics, whose words survived. Now the path widens to the school before them, and it begins with its founder, whose words almost all vanished. Today: Diogenes Laërtius.
screen: `A LONG LIST OF TITLES.` → `KNOWN ONLY THROUGH OTHERS.` → `THE FOUNDER'S LOST BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, who he was. Zeno came from Citium, a town on Cyprus, and made his way to Athens. The story, told by the biographer Diogenes Laërtius, is that he was a merchant who lost his cargo in a shipwreck, and in Athens found philosophy. He studied with the Cynic Crates and others, and then taught in a painted colonnade on the edge of the marketplace, the Stoa Poikilē. His followers were called the people of the stoa, the porch: Stoics. Second, the books. Diogenes Laërtius lists Zeno's titles in book seven of his Lives: a Republic, On Life according to Nature, On the Passions, On What Is Appropriate, On Law, and more. Not one survives whole. What we have are scraps: a sentence quoted here, a summary there, mostly by later writers, some of them critics. Third, what that means. Everything we've been calling Stoicism this year, we've learned from people writing centuries after Zeno. We know the founder the way you know a great-great-grandparent: through stories, a few sayings, and family resemblance. And some of Zeno's ideas were apparently embarrassing to later Stoics, especially parts of his Republic, and they may have smoothed them over. Fourth, the strange comfort. Zeno's words mostly vanished, and the school was still alive centuries later, when Marcus wrote. What survived wasn't his sentences. It was what his students did with them.
screen: `FROM CITIUM, BY WAY OF A SHIPWRECK.` · `A LIST OF TITLES, NONE SURVIVING.` · `KNOWN THROUGH LATER WRITERS.` · `WHAT LASTED: WHAT STUDENTS DID.` · then, large: `MOSTLY LOST.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Suppose that a hundred years from now, almost nothing you made survives. No files, no photos. Only what people remember of how you were. Ask yourself: what would you want to be carried on? Not a sentence or an achievement. A way of being: patient with your kids, honest at work, the friend who showed up. Let one thing come forward. Hold it for a few breaths. That's the part of you that doesn't depend on paper. The bell holds the time.
Zeno, the shipwrecked merchant who found philosophy in Athens and taught in a painted colonnade, though almost none of his own books survive. Today's word.
Your line: mostly lost. Today, do one small thing in the way you'd want remembered, the way that lasts even when the words don't. Day six hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Students of Stoicism read Zeno through the fragments and reports gathered from later writers, especially Diogenes Laërtius's Lives, book seven.

original.note: Greek: the painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught, which gave the Stoics their name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the founder of Stoicism wrote its great books.
what it means: Zeno wrote many books, and almost all are lost; we know him through others.
what a scholar hears: Zeno's fragments were gathered by Hans von Arnim in Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta (1903–1905), and ancient reports suggest later Stoics were uneasy with parts of his Republic.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
Hans von Arnim (ed.), Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta

notes: Zeno of Citium c. 334–262 BC; arrival in Athens c. 312 and teaching from c. 300 BC. 'Around 300 BC' is hedged; confirm.
Titles from DL 7.4: Republic, On Life according to Nature, On Impulse or Human Nature, On the Passions, On Duty (the appropriate, kathēkon), On Law, etc. Confirm titles used.
Later Stoics' discomfort with Zeno's Republic: DL 7.32–34 reports critics and some Stoics who called it spurious or early. Hedged; confirm.
'The school lasted five hundred years' (c. 300 BC to the 3rd century AD) is approximate; confirm.
